title: Odor vocabularies diverge in codability but converge in valence and edibility
abstract: Abstract Odors are often difficult to describe, but culturally distinct languages differ in their capacity to express odor experiences. Some languages contain several abstract odor terms expressing odor qualities directly, and thus have odor vocabularies that are high in abstraction. This might allow for a high between-speaker consistency – that is, codability – in the description of odors. Which aspects of odor descriptions are consistent and which are variable across languages? We hypothesized that cross-linguistic differences in abstraction and codability coexist with cross-cultural similarities on a deeper semantic level, such that odors are primarily differentiated in terms of valence (pleasant vs. unpleasant) and edibility (edible vs. inedible). No comprehensive cross-linguistic comparison of such odor-semantic organization exists to date. We compare vocabularies for imagined odors of seven languages (Cantonese, English, Polish, Russian, Spanish, Swedish and Turkish). Over 40 speakers of each language ( N = 358) provided odor descriptors of 121 imagined odors. We analyzed the abstraction, codability, valence and edibility of the resulting vocabularies, comparing their between-odor and between-language variability and their language pair convergence. Odor vocabularies diverge in codability, but converge in valence and edibility. These findings indicate that although languages differ with respect to their encoding of imagined odors, they share the same odor-semantic organization.
